title: CeresAI Dedicated Onramp & Burst Tolerance Discovery
summary: Intro discovery call to qualify CeresAI's need for reserved GPU capacity, isolation requirements for multi-tenant models, burst handling and scaling expectations. Key concerns: data residency, KMS integration, warm pool prewarm times, and SLA for tail latency. Next steps agreed: sizing spreadsheet, security packet, and a short latency proof-of-concept runbook.
action_items: Alex Park (AE): Share customized reserved-capacity pricing and burst-sizing spreadsheet (due: 2025-08-14)
Maya Chen (SE): Draft POC runbook for 48-hour tail-latency benchmark and prewarm profiling (due: 2025-08-13)
Sarah Lee (Customer Security): Send list of compliance docs they need (SOC2 evidence, KMS integrations) (due: 2025-08-12)
Ben Ortiz (Customer): Provide expected RPS distribution and 95/99 latency targets and model sizes (due: 2025-08-12)
next_steps: Schedule POC kickoff (48-hour perf test) for week of 2025-08-18
AE to send pricing + contract template
SE to prepare runbook and remote profiling checklist
Customer to share synthetic traffic profile and security checklist
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-08-10
Time: 15:00 PDT (UTC-7)
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Alex Park (Redwood AE), Maya Chen (Redwood SE), Diego Ramos (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (CeresAI Head of ML), Ben Ortiz (Platform), Sarah Lee (Security), Owen Park (CTO)
Shared artifacts: preliminary pricing sheet (link: drive.redwood/pricing/ceresai), security one-pager (link), burst-sizing template (link)

[00:00] Alex Park: Hey everyone thanks for joining, I'm Alex from Redwood, this is Maya and Diego from our solutions team. hows everyone doing?
[00:05] Priya Nair: good thanks, busy week but excited to chat, appreciate you fitting us in.
[00:10] Alex Park: cool. high level, we want to understand a few things — your current serving footprint, what peak windows look like, whether you need full physical isolation, and what latency/cost tradeoffs you're willing to take during bursts. if we can cover that we can propose dedicated vs hybrid reserved approach.
[00:25] Owen Park: yeah gimme a sec, I'll flag the core asks — reliability at 99th percentile, predictable unit cost, and encryption for model inputs at rest and in flight. also we need to keep the private deployment option open for a subset of regulated customers.
[00:40] Ben Ortiz: current infra is GKE on GCP, we run inference on a mix of spot and reserved GPU instances with Triton on top. but ops overhead is huge — packing, eviction mitigation, and then cold-starts on larger models kill tail latency.
[00:55] Maya Chen: got it. when you say "larger models" — what sizes are you running in prod? are these 7B-ish or bigger like 30B?
[01:05] Priya Nair: mostly 13B and some 30B variants for our contextual generation pipelines. single-turn requests, average token length around 60 but some sessions go long. throughput-wise we usually have 200 rps steady, spikes to ~2k for a few minutes during nightly batch and marketing events.
[01:25] Diego Ramos: that burst factor is useful — 10x from steady. do you have predictable spike windows or are they spiky/unpredictable?
[01:32] Priya Nair: a mix, predictable for scheduled jobs, but marketing-triggered traffic is unpredictable. we need a fail-safe so customer-facing features don't degrade.
[01:40] Alex Park: that's a classic reserved plus burst use-case. Redwood Dedicated lets you reserve baseline capacity and then configure burst pools and warm pools for prewarmed instances. tradeoffs are cost vs how much you keep hot.
[01:52] Sarah Lee: quick security question — we require KMS integration (customer-managed keys), audit logs that show model access per-tenant, and SSO with SCIM/SAML. can you support private keying?
[02:03] Maya Chen: yes — KMS/HSM integrations are supported in Private and Dedicated with our enterprise package. audit logs are token-level — we surface which model and which route generated requests, timestamps, and full event logs that can be exported. SCIM provisioning + SAML SSO is available. we'll share the security packet after the call.
[02:18] Owen Park: is that the same for Hosted? because some of our teams would prefer a hosted path first to move faster.
[02:25] Alex Park: hosted has a different trust model — we can do KMS for hosted but with constraints; customer-managed keys and fully private control plane are offered on Private deployments. Dedicated gives strong isolation (dedicated GPU pools) without the overhead of managing OS-level infra.
[02:40] Ben Ortiz: about isolation — we have multi-tenant customers and some require physical isolation. can we pin certain customers to dedicated nodes?
[02:50] Diego Ramos: yes, Dedicated supports tenant fencing where you can map tenants to reserved nodes. you can also set guardrails so noisy tenants can't exceed quota. there's a policy layer for preemption and tenancy.
[03:02] Priya Nair: preemption is a worry — we can't have model inference evicted mid-request. what does Redwood guarantee there?
[03:10] Maya Chen: Dedicated reserved nodes are non-preemptible. burst capacity can run on shared pools and we have graceful eviction and fallback policies; for example, automatic routing to smaller-quantized variants or to hosted fallback with a slightly higher latency but preserved correctness. those policies are configurable.
[03:27] Alex Park: to add — you can pin critical customers to strict non-preemptible nodes and allow others to use burst pools. during rollouts you can have canary rules that protect traffic.
[03:38] Ben Ortiz: sounds good. on the burst behavior — what are typical prewarm times for 13B/30B models? we've seen warmup times of minutes to tens of minutes in our infra.
[03:49] Diego Ramos: depends on quantization and kernel selection. in our infra a 13B with Q4/8 and warmed KV cache can be ready in under a minute for first tokens, 30B sometimes 3-6 minutes if cold. warm pools reduce this — we keep instances with KV caches populated for expected prompts. we can show historical heatmaps from similar customers.
[04:10] Priya Nair: heatmaps would be helpful. also we care about tail latency — 99.9th. how do you instrument and what SLOs do you typically hit?
[04:20] Maya Chen: we provide token-level latency breakdowns, per-route dashboards, and percentiles. For Dedicated customers we commonly observe 95th under 120ms for Llama-derivatives at small batch sizes; 99/99.9 depends on workload — we'll run an initial profiling POC to set realistic SLOs.
[04:36] Owen Park: ok, cost is top of mind. if we reserve a baseline what does billing look like for bursts? flat overage, per-token?
[04:45] Alex Park: reserved capacity is monthly committed (node-hour pricing). Burst usage is billed on top at a lower per-minute price for on-demand nodes and per-token for hosted fallback. We also offer commitment tiers that reduce burst premiums. We'll send the pricing matrix.
[04:58] Ben Ortiz: can we ramp capacity automatically when RPS rises? we don't want to manually intervene in the middle of an event.
[05:06] Diego Ramos: yes — autoscaling with policies. you can set up autoscale to scale on queue depth, GPU utilization, or combined signals. critical is the warm-pool sizing and prewarm triggers — autoscale will request more nodes but prewarming determines how fast they are useful.
[05:22] Priya Nair: what's the recommended warm-pool size for a 2k spike from 200 steady?
[05:28] Maya Chen: a starting heuristic is to keep ~30% of expected spike capacity warm for quick bursts and rely on autoscale for the remainder. for your profile, keep enough to handle a 5x spike instantly, and allow autoscale to fill to 10x with a short higher-latency tail. we'll validate with the POC.
[05:42] Sarah Lee: compliance: if some customers require on-prem-only, how hard is migration from Dedicated to Private or on-prem? we need the path documented.
[05:51] Alex Park: we provide a migration plan — Dedicated and Private share the same control plane APIs; moving to Private includes a setup for VPC/air-gapped environments and KMS handover. it's not trivial but we have runbooks and professional services to help.
[06:04] Priya Nair: great. can you outline what's in the POC? I want measurable criteria — e.g. sustained 2k rps for 30 minutes with 99p under X ms, warm-pool effectiveness, and cost delta.
[06:16] Maya Chen: sure — proposed POC: 48-hour test with: 1) synthetic traffic profile replay of your production traces, 2) warm pool enabled at several sizes, 3) measure 95/99/99.9 latency, throughput, prewarm times, and cost per token. we'll also test fallback routing to hosted and quantized model variants.
[06:30] Ben Ortiz: how intrusive is the POC? do we need to change our infra or provide logs?
[06:36] Diego Ramos: minimally intrusive. we just need an ingress endpoint and synthetic traffic; if you want deeper profiling we'll request temporary access to metrics or a profiling agent. otherwise we can run blackbox throughput tests against a mirror.
[06:50] Owen Park: about network egress and data residency — some EU customers require data never leaves region. can dedicated pools be region pinned?
[06:59] Alex Park: absolutely — you can pin to regions and restrict routing. Private deployments are ideal if you must keep data inside a VPC or on-prem. Dedicated can be region-specific as well.
[07:10] Priya Nair: any gotchas on tokenization or prompt prefix caching? we use long-context prompts sometimes.
[07:18] Maya Chen: prefix/K-V cache is supported; it's one of our cache layers for repeated contexts. long context increases memory and may affect batching efficiency; our kernel selector adapts but we typically recommend quantization and shorter effective context windows for tail-latency critical paths.
[07:34] Ben Ortiz: are there circuit-breakers or rate-limiting we'll need to add client-side?
[07:39] Diego Ramos: we provide rate-limiting tiers, token-level quotas, and client-side backoff recommendations. you can enforce per-tenant quotas to protect baseline capacity.
[07:50] Priya Nair: one more — model versioning and rollouts. we need to be able to pin traffic to versions and rollback fast if a newer model degrades quality.
[07:59] Maya Chen: rollouts are first-class — canary deploys, A/B, and automatic fallback rules based on model-level metrics. you can pin endpoints to specific model versions. we'll show the Console flow in a demo.
[08:11] Alex Park: wrapping up, sounds like next steps are: we'll send the pricing and POC runbook, customer provides traffic profile and security doc list, schedule POC for week of Aug 18. any last questions?
[08:21] Sarah Lee: just want the security packet, and a note on KMS integration specifics.
[08:25] Alex Park: will include that.
[08:27] Priya Nair: ok thanks everyone.
[08:30] Owen Park: thanks, talk soon.

End notes: call had typical transcription noise — some product names mis-transcribed. agreed measurable POC and clear deliverables.
